seoTitle: Free Docker Compose to Kubernetes Manifest Converter
metaDescription: Convert a docker-compose.yml into Kubernetes Deployments, Services, PersistentVolumeClaims and Secrets. Free, runs in your browser, nothing uploaded.
intro: Converts a docker-compose.yml into Kubernetes YAML: a Deployment per service, Services for ports, PersistentVolumeClaims for named volumes and optionally a Secret. Unsupported features are listed as NOTE comments.
why: Compose is the easy way to describe a multi-container app on one machine, and when it is time to move to Kubernetes the manifests have to be rewritten. Each service needs a Deployment, ports need a Service, named volumes need claims, and secrets should not sit in plain environment variables. This tool drafts all of that from your compose file: images, commands, environment, replicas and resource limits from deploy.resources, a healthcheck turned into a liveness probe, and optional Secrets for variables whose names look sensitive. Things with no direct equivalent, such as depends_on, build, env_file and bind mounts, are noted as comments instead of being silently dropped. Treat the result as a starting point. It runs in your browser.
howTo: Paste your docker-compose.yml into the input box.
Set a namespace, the Service type for published ports and the PVC size, and choose whether to create a Secret.
Read the NOTE comments, adjust the manifests and apply them to a test cluster first.

faq.a: Services become Deployments with image, command, environment, replicas and resources. Published or exposed ports become Services. Named volumes become PersistentVolumeClaims. A healthcheck becomes a livenessProbe.
depends_on, build, env_file and bind mounts have no direct equivalent, so they are listed as NOTE comments. You must replace them, for example with an image build pipeline and ConfigMaps.

faq.q: How does the Secret option work?
faq.a: Variables whose names look like passwords, tokens or keys are moved to a Secret and referenced from the Deployment. Review the list, since detection is by name.
No. It is a starting point. Add readiness probes, resource requests, ingress, security settings and proper storage classes before you rely on it.
